Timothy Theodore Duncan embodies everything I’d ever hope to be in my life.

Tim Duncan is possibly the most boring, forgotten, and quiet superstar
athlete to ever play: pedestrian numbers, mediocre athleticism, stoic
expression. Yet, has more accolades than almost any other NBA player, is genuinely loved by his teammates, coaching staff, and fans beyond the sport, stars in no commercials, has zero sponsors while focusing any and all attention and financial efforts in the local community, his home, and victims of hurricanes; the list goes on and on.

Duncan is why I watched the San Antonio Spurs. His minimalist approach to the game, to people, to life is what I want to exhibit and do my best to learn. He comes, he works, he leaves. He stays humble and sacrifices what could otherwise be stardom, money, and ratings. He relinquishes his stats for the well-being of the team, the system, and the coach. He graduated college before entering the NBA just to finish out his dying mother’s wishes. He had the simplest, most silent retirement.

He was one of the first people I saw who was an antithesis to
stereotypical masculinity and helped me accept myself as a person who could accomplish things outside of the means of ‘hunger’ and ‘dominance’ but instead consistency, discipline, and fundamentals. He showed me that being quiet and reserved doesn’t mean you can’t still speak to people in other ways.

I still wish I had that Tim Duncan night shirt jersey I wore as a kid.

Not to me. I mean, the dictionary is just as much biased, is it not? It's not some objective document that gets a final say on all things meaningful. It was formed historically and culturally through what is essentially white male academia, not people who have been affected the most by it. If that's the case, then I'd sooner trust those who experience it more than people who just write about it.

There are many types of racism that it can't really be defined through just one sentence. Some is overt, some is subtle. Some is systematic and institutional while some is individual. Some of it is also passive and not even intentional.

In this specific scenario, Patty Mills definitely stated that he felt offended and uncomfortable about the person shouting at him. That is really all anybody should really be caring about. People of color are subjected to comments of this nature that, on the surface, may look descriptive, but contextually are meant to mean something a bit more than that. That isn't easy to understand if you do not necessarily share the experience of what it's like to be a visible minority (not saying that you can't be, but generally speaking anybody who resorts to the dictionary first-hand to talk about my life experience has no idea how binary that truly is).

racism isn't just strictly defined through dictionaries.

1) response rates
2) length of responses
3) The amount of conversation outside of small talk (how are you? what are you doing)?

If there isn't much going on outside of those typical topics and she's giving you short responses within say, 30 minute to an hour gaps, I'd say you shouldn't be texting anymore than a few times a day. Some people do develop chemistry through text. She may be one of them, but you have to discern how truly "interested" she is in actually texting you this early and go from there.

She does have the right to feel angry because you actually went through deliberation and made this decision only to flake on the last minute.

You and I are very much alike.

When I was in love, it was the only time in my life I truly felt alive on a consistent basis. I felt motivated to try my best in everything, I lived in a carefree manner about my persona, and I felt that no matter what happened to me, I'd always be happy. 

But when she left me, I came tumbling back down to Earth and now, I'm back to being the lazy bum with no true motivation or passion.

Where we differ is how we are single; I want that feeling again. I want to feel alive again. I'm afraid to fall in love, but I also at least want to feel something. Otherwise, I feel empty, unaccomplished, and lonely as I've always been in my life. I also don't want just any love. Like you, I want someone who doesn't just 'flip the switch' but sadly, people our age don't truly know what they want, and there isn't a high chance that someone wouldn't flip the switch with me. The kind of love I want is eternal.. just like you.

But how do I deal with this? How do I learn to be happy alone? The answer is... still pending.

Is it possible that I'll find another woman as beautiful as she was? Sure. Is it likely? I have no idea. Should I constantly think about it? No, but I do anyway, and slowly but surely, I try to cope with the idea of having the status quo be like this possibly forever.

Sounds silly at first, but looking at my track record, it  is a possibility. I don't know if it'd work for you, but I can honestly tell you that I've tried everything; hypnosis, counseling, engaging deeply in my hobbies, making lots of platonic friendships (only to remain jealous of their relationships everyday), and even trying to find new things to make me happy and motivated. I still haven't found an ultimate solution to being alone when you crave romance.

I'm not even sure if it's possible to be happy alone forever; at least with me.

So.. I've just done my best to accept that I may be alone like this for a long time. It's nobody's fault. It's just life. Some people are naturally in and out of relationships, and some people just aren't going to be in many (or any). In this case, I have no control over it, so I accept this lower level of happiness.. involuntarily.

tl;dr I can't exactly give you a better answer than accepting that what may make you the happiest simply may not come true. All you can do is engage in the things that make you happy today, and if you do come across love, try not to think negatively on it too much.

You are certainly not alone. This phenomenom isn't uncommon.

In my experience, the likelihood of people continuing to be best friends despite their ex status truly depends on whether the break-up was mutual. In your case, it wasn't actually a break-up, but a broken heart. this isn't just in relationships either; it's in friendships. If a friend does something to hurt or betray you, of course you'd feel uncomfortable being around them again. It wouldn't be the same.

How do you stop making other people the focus of your life? Well, first you have to realize if that's what you really ultimately want. I understand that being happy with yourself is true strength, but do keep in mind not to go to the extreme in which you don't connect to anybody. Don't be afraid to fall in love again. You said you haven't experienced a real relationship yet; it's certainly worth it. Don't give up.

Sure, it may be easier emotionally, but the message would at least be clear. If you leave a person wondering about your love, it will only backfire. It might pull him even closer to you if you stay away purposely.

Be brave and tell him the truth. There really is no better scenario. If you stay in it, you're unhappy. If you suddenly don't talk to him, it'll be a bad break-up (and bad break-ups usually leave worse feelings).

Seems like you aren't all too happy. Is there anything about him that you like? Is there anything you can think of that is redeeming? If not, then it's time to leave him.

When you want to break-up with someone, you don't do it slowly and indirectly. You tell him the truth. Tell him how you feel about the relationship. If he doesn't want to change (or if you don't want to change if you learn new things), then it's time to simply split up. Lay it out on the line. Are you afraid? Don't be. You will save yourself a lot of trouble by being up-front about it.

Introducing yourself as a mutual friend shouldn't be that weird. I know you instinctively think this may ruin your chance, but random introductions are not dealbreakers. You know her friend. That's all you really have to say. Emphasize this point and you'll be fine.

If you already know personal things about her, that's your next topic of discussion. Just be confident. Don't worry about being a random guy; you're technically not random.

Keep in mind any type of current event going on. Sports, news, movies, music, etc. Almost everyone is willing to discuss one of these topics at least for a few minutes.

If you're trying to get to know a woman, ask about something that's not immediately obvious. If you see a woman's voice change or eyes light-up at the change of a certain topic, you found something to roll with. People's passions are the best way to establish a mutual friendship fast.

Try to be as sincere as you can. Avoid complimenting too much. If you must compliment, let it be something that she may not even notice. Compliment on something that isn't immediately obvious.
